subject: Architecture
title: The Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge: Longest on Earth
description: A fast breakdown of The Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge: Longest on Earth for builders.

hook.text: At 102 miles long, China's Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge is the longest bridge in the world.

buildup.text: It carries high-speed rail between Shanghai and Nanjing, crossing rivers, canals, lakes, and rice paddies.

discovery.text: 10,000 workers built it in just four years. Over 450,000 tons of structural steel were used.

twist.text: The bridge crosses Yangcheng Lake on a nine-mile stretch — trains appear to glide across the water.

climax.text: China has six of the world's ten longest bridges. Infrastructure at this scale exists nowhere else.

punchline.text: It would take over an hour to walk the length. By train, it's 30 minutes.

quiz.question: How long is the Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge?

details.summary: The Danyang-Kunshan Grand Bridge in China stretches 164.8 kilometers — the longest bridge on Earth. Built in just four years for the Beijing-Shanghai High-Speed Railway, it crosses rivers, canals, lakes.
details.whyItMatters: This bridge demonstrates industrial-scale construction at unprecedented speed and length. Prefabrication and specialized machinery enabled 10,000 workers to build 164.8 kilometers of elevated railway in just four years.
takeaways: At 164.8 km it is the longest bridge on Earth
Built in four years for Beijing-Shanghai high-speed rail
Prefabricated segments were assembled by specialized machinery

faq.question: Why build a bridge instead of laying track on the ground?
faq.answer: An elevated viaduct protects the rail line from ground-level flooding, settlement, and interference with farmland and roads below. It also maintains the precise geometry that high-speed trains require — even slight ground settlement could derail a train traveling at 300 km/h.

faq.question: How were segments placed so quickly?
faq.answer: Massive girder-launching machines straddled completed sections and placed 900-ton prefabricated box girders onto piers. Each machine could place one span per day. Multiple machines worked simultaneously along different sections of the route to achieve the rapid construction timeline.
